title: UK Banks Trim AI Risk as Regulator Warns of Sector Alarm
summary: Bank of England supervisor Katharine Braddick reveals UK banks are reducing AI exposure amid growing sector concerns. New guidance on frontier AI risks coming.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- UK banks are actively reducing AI exposure as sector alarm intensifies, confirmed by Bank of England's top supervisor Katharine Braddick in November 2026.
- The BOE's Prudential Regulation Authority will publish concrete guidance on frontier AI and quantum computing risks later this month.
- Banks are reassessing client relationships and risk appetite independently, with regulators monitoring but not imposing capital rule changes yet.


UK banks have begun actively reducing their exposure to artificial intelligence as alarm mounts over a potential sector correction, according to the Bank of England's top banking supervisor. In her first interview since taking the helm of the Prudential Regulation Authority in July 2026, Katharine Braddick confirmed that lenders are reassessing their AI-related client relationships and risk appetite in response to growing market volatility.


The acknowledgment marks a significant shift in how traditional financial institutions are approaching AI investments following months of turbulence in the sector. While the BOE's extensive interrogation of banks' AI exposure hasn't revealed that lenders would amplify any AI shock, regulators are maintaining heightened vigilance.


## Banks Self-Regulating AI Exposure


Braddick revealed that banks are independently trimming their AI exposure without regulatory mandate. "We're all alarmed at the moment, aren't we?" she said, describing a retrenchment she's observed recently among UK financial institutions. Banks are "all asking themselves that question" of whether to reduce exposure, with firms reconsidering their risk appetite on a client-by-client basis.


The supervisor noted she can "see firms looking at their risk appetite and thinking and considering, 'Yes this client, not that client.' You do see it feed through." Despite this trend, the BOE is not currently planning to use capital rules to encourage lower exposures, allowing banks to make their own risk management decisions.


## New Guidance on Frontier AI Risks


The PRA and Financial Conduct Authority will publish guidance later in November 2026 on managing risks from frontier AI and quantum computing. Officially released on November 10, 2026, Braddick's comments preview what she described as a "quite concrete" approach that will include specific governance expectations for financial institutions.


The regulator hopes the guidance will initiate an "iterative exercise" leading to deeper partnerships between the BOE and the banking industry. This comes months after Anthropic's Mythos model spooked watchdogs globally, forcing governments to contemplate unprecedented cyberattacks perpetrated by agentic AI systems.


## Operational Resilience Takes Priority


Beyond AI-specific concerns, Braddick emphasized that operational resilience has become paramount in her conversations with bank chief executives. The PRA is working to operationalize the "minimum viable bank" framework proposed by BOE Governor Andrew Bailey earlier in 2026, a concept requiring banks to maintain "bare metal" functions capable of delivering continuous service during cyberattacks.


"It's an urgent question," Braddick said of deliberations on which banks should be required to have their own infrastructure, as well as how to create structures for smaller lenders who can't afford independent rails. No deadlines have been set for introducing such rules, but the work is viewed as critical to UK competitiveness.


## Market Context and Sector Volatility


The banking sector's AI caution comes amid broader market turbulence. The US midterm elections drove a sell-off in AI-related stocks, causing a rout that has imperiled Anthropic's anticipated public offering. This volatility has prompted financial institutions to reassess their exposure across the AI ecosystem, from direct investments to client relationships with AI companies.


Braddick, a Cambridge graduate who spent nearly two decades in policy before a three-year stint at Barclays, noted that AI risks are now a "constant conversation" within the regulatory sphere and among bank leadership teams.


## What This Means


The Bank of England's confirmation that UK banks are independently reducing AI exposure signals a maturing risk management approach to artificial intelligence in traditional finance. While regulators are not mandating capital requirement changes, the upcoming guidance on[frontier AI risks](https://emergent.sh/glossary/catastrophic-risk) will establish concrete governance frameworks that could influence global banking standards. The self-imposed retrenchment by lenders suggests the financial sector is taking AI-related risks seriously, even as the technology continues to reshape business operations. For banks, the challenge will be balancing innovation opportunities with prudent risk management in an increasingly volatile AI landscape.
